name: alpaka (alpaka3 BabelStream)
baseline: NVIDIA reference BabelStream implementation (native OpenMP on Grace CPU, native CUDA on GH200 GPU)
workload: BabelStream Copy/Mult/Add/Triad/Dot memory-bandwidth kernels, double precision, 1.073742 billion elements, run through alpaka3's portable kernel API versus native reference code and mainline alpaka.
claimed_speedup: On NVIDIA Grace CPU (OpenMP, 72 threads, GNU 14.3, -ftree-vectorize -mcpu=neoverse-v2): alpaka3 reaches 107% of the NVIDIA reference throughput on average over the common kernels (alpaka3 Copy 469, Mult 469, Add 453, Triad 456 GB/s; Dot 447 GB/s for alpaka3 versus 40 GB/s for mainline alpaka; no Dot reference). On NVIDIA GH200 GPU (CUDA 13.3): 99% of the NVIDIA reference on average (alpaka3 Copy 3,636, Mult 3,634, Add 3,665, Triad 3,667 GB/s; Dot 3,731 GB/s versus 3,678 GB/s for mainline alpaka), i.e. parity, not a win.
compiler_and_flags: CPU run: GNU 14.3, -ftree-vectorize -mcpu=neoverse-v2 (from chart footer); GPU run: CUDA 13.3, flags not stated
hardware: JUPITER at the Juelich Supercomputing Centre: NVIDIA Grace CPU (72 OpenMP threads) and NVIDIA GH200 GPU
tradeoffs: Single-source performance-portability layer (CUDA, HIP, SYCL, OpenMP, serial backends) that has to match hand-written native kernels; alpaka3 on the default branch is a redesign with a different API from mainline alpaka. Explicit shared-memory caching is left to the kernel author.
caveats: The numbers exist only as two SVG charts embedded in the README (text rendered as paths); values above were read from rendered images. The 'NVIDIA reference' bars are described as 'the mean of supplied runs', so the baseline was not re-run by the project and its build and flags are not stated. Benchmark source is public in benchmark/babelstream but the README has no instructions to reproduce. The GPU result is parity (99%), only the CPU run is faster (107%, i.e. about 7%), and Dot has no reference. The old listed repo ComputationalRadiationPhysics/alpaka now only redirects to alpaka-group/alpaka, and the listed LGPLv3+ licence is outdated (now MPL-2.0). Only memory-bandwidth kernels are measured, no thread-pool or scheduling workload despite the suggested category.

name: Boehm GC (Boehm-Demers-Weiser collector)
workload: Multi-threaded variant of the Boehm GC allocation benchmark (GCBench-style, almost entirely small-object allocation), elapsed seconds, collector versus a malloc/free version of the same client.
claimed_speedup: GC thread-unsafe 9 s versus glibc malloc/free 10.51 s (pthreads not linked); GC thread-safe 10.3 s versus 20.90 s for malloc/free (one thread, pthreads linked); two clients 23.5 s versus 24.55 s. Ratios 1.17x, 2.03x and 1.04x (derived from page data). Docs also state 'for programs allocating primarily very small objects, the collector may be faster; for programs allocating primarily large objects it will be slower' and that with thread-local allocation it 'may in some cases significantly outperform malloc/free'.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (collector built with -D GC_THREADS for the thread-safe rows)
hardware: Dual-processor Pentium III/500 under Linux 2.2.12 (year-2000 collector release)
tradeoffs: Conservative, non-moving, non-real-time collector: pauses grow with heap size, pointer-free data should use GC_malloc_atomic, memory from system malloc is invisible to it, and large-object workloads are slower than malloc/free.
caveats: First-party measurement from about 2000 on a Pentium III with a collector release that is 'ancient' per the page; the page itself says the benchmark 'favors a garbage collector, since most objects are small' and that results are 'very sensitive to both hardware and OS issues'. Compiler, flags and benchmark source are not in the repo docs (the gc_bench page lives on hboehm.info, which was not reachable here). Third-party evidence cited by the docs (Detlefs, Dosser and Zorn, 'Memory Allocation Costs in Large C and C++ Programs') could not be opened, so it is not used. The repo is now bdwgc/bdwgc (listed ivmai/bdwgc redirects). The licence is the project's own MIT-style licence (SPDX Boehm-GC).

name: Boost.Fiber (boost::fibers, from Boost)
workload: Skynet microbenchmark ported to Boost.Fiber: spawn a tree of 10 children per node down to 1,000,000 execution units that return and sum their ordinals; reported as average time per fiber versus per pthread, std::thread and std::async (threads limited to 10,000 units because 1,000,000 exhausted resources).
claimed_speedup: Time per execution unit: fiber 0.05-0.09 us (16C/32T, work stealing, tcmalloc) and 1.69-1.79 us (1C/1T, round robin, tcmalloc), versus pthread 54-73 us, std::thread 52-73 us, std::async 106-122 us; Go goroutines 0.42-0.49 us, Erlang 0.63-0.73 us, Haskell 0.05-0.06 us. Roughly 30-40x less per unit single-threaded and several hundred to about 1,500 times with work stealing (derived from page data). Separate repo boostorg/context documents the underlying switch: fcontext 9 ns / 19 cycles versus ucontext_t 547 ns / 1130 cycles.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-6.3.1, b2 variant=release optimization=speed (public Jamfile.v2 in performance/fiber and performance/thread); tcmalloc via -ltcmalloc for the fiber rows
hardware: Dual Intel Xeon E5 2620v4 2.2GHz, 16C/32T, 64GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: Cooperative scheduling: a fiber must yield explicitly and blocking system calls stall its thread; needs Boost.Context; each fiber needs its own stack (fixedsize_stack used in the benchmark); allocator choice matters a lot in multi-threaded runs.
caveats: Not like for like: fiber rows are averaged over 1,000,000 units while thread rows are averaged over 10,000 (1,000,000 threads could not be spawned), threads use 8 kB stacks for pthread versus 1-2 MB for std::thread, and the fiber rows use tcmalloc. The 0.05-0.09 us figure needs 16C/32T work stealing; single-thread it is 1.69-1.79 us. The doc is from 2017 (gcc-6.3.1, Haskell/Go/Erlang versions of that year). Flags are given as b2 features, not literal -O options. Chosen as Boost's strongest documented comparison of system threading baselines; other Boost components were not examined (Boost.Context, a separate repo, has the cleaner fcontext versus ucontext_t switch comparison and could be seeded on its own).
